exercises.title: Network Effects in Digital Markets
exercises.passage:
Some products become more useful as more people adopt them, a phenomenon economists call a network effect. A telephone network illustrates the basic idea: a single telephone has little value, whereas a network connecting millions of users is highly useful. Digital platforms can exhibit similar effects because additional users may attract more sellers, developers, or content creators.

However, network effects do not guarantee permanent dominance. Users may switch when a rival offers substantially better technology, when several platforms can be used simultaneously, or when the cost of moving data and contacts is low. Consequently, firms often attempt to strengthen network effects by making their services compatible with complementary products while simultaneously increasing switching costs.

Policymakers pay close attention to such strategies because strong network effects can produce efficiency gains but may also make entry more difficult for competitors. The economic significance of network effects therefore depends not simply on the number of users but on the structure of interactions among users, complementary suppliers, and competing platforms.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To explain how network effects operate and why their consequences vary
To argue that digital platforms should always be regulated
To compare telephone prices across different markets
To show that new technology inevitably replaces established firms
questions.explanation: The passage defines network effects, qualifies their power, and ends by saying their significance depends on structure — it explains rather than argues for regulation.

questions.stem: The word "dominance" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: compatibility
control
innovation
cooperation
questions.explanation: Permanent dominance = lasting control of a market.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which condition can make switching platforms easier?
options: High costs of transferring contacts
A large number of complementary suppliers
Low costs of moving data
Strong compatibility with existing products
questions.explanation: Users may switch "when the cost of moving data and contacts is low". High transfer costs would do the opposite.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention policymakers?
options: To show that network effects have implications for competition
To suggest that governments create most digital platforms
To explain how telephone networks are financed
To argue that switching costs are always harmful
questions.explanation: Policymakers watch these strategies because they can make entry harder for competitors.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the final sentence?
options: User numbers alone are insufficient to evaluate a network effect
Large platforms always prevent market entry
Complementary suppliers reduce the usefulness of platforms
Network effects matter only in digital industries
questions.explanation: "Not simply on the number of users but on the structure of interactions" means the count of users is not enough.

exercises.title: The Puzzle of Bird Navigation
exercises.passage:
Each autumn, many songbirds fly thousands of kilometers to wintering grounds they have never seen, often traveling alone and at night. How such inexperienced migrants find their way has long puzzled biologists. Early experiments showed that caged birds orient themselves in the correct seasonal direction even when they cannot see the sky, suggesting that they possess an internal compass sensitive to Earth's magnetic field.

The mechanism behind this compass remains contested. One hypothesis locates it in iron-rich cells in the beak; another proposes that light triggers chemical reactions in the eye whose outcome depends on the orientation of the magnetic field. The second hypothesis gained support when researchers found that weak radio-frequency noise, which should disrupt such reactions but not iron-based sensors, disoriented birds in the laboratory.

Yet a compass alone does not explain navigation. Young birds that are displaced experimentally tend to continue in their original direction and miss their destination, whereas experienced adults often correct their course. This difference implies that adults have learned a kind of map, perhaps built from magnetic gradients, smells, or landmarks, that allows them to determine where they are, not merely which way they are facing.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that caged birds orient correctly without seeing the sky?
options: To show that birds rely mainly on the stars
To support the idea that birds can sense magnetic direction
To argue that captivity changes migratory behavior
To explain why young birds travel alone
questions.explanation: Orientation without the sky suggests an internal magnetic compass.

questions.stem: The word "contested" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: disputed
unknown
proven
complicated
questions.explanation: Two competing hypotheses are presented, so the mechanism is disputed.

questions.stem: Why did the radio-frequency experiment support the eye-based hypothesis?
options: The noise damaged iron-rich cells in the beak
The noise should affect light-dependent reactions but not iron-based sensors
Birds exposed to the noise could still navigate perfectly
The noise only disoriented birds that were kept in the dark
questions.explanation: The disturbance should interfere only with the chemical mechanism, so the disorientation points to that mechanism.

questions.stem: What does the displacement experiment suggest about young birds?
options: They have no magnetic compass
They lack a learned map that would let them correct their position
They navigate better than adults
They depend entirely on smell
questions.explanation: Young birds keep their original heading and miss the target; adults correct, implying a learned map that juveniles lack.

questions.stem: How is the passage organized?
options: A problem is stated, a proposed explanation is evaluated, and a remaining limitation is identified
Two species are compared and then contrasted with a third
A historical account is followed by a prediction about future research
A theory is described and then completely rejected
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the puzzle, paragraph 2 weighs compass mechanisms, paragraph 3 shows that a compass alone is insufficient.

exercises.title: Roman Concrete
exercises.passage:
Many Roman harbors, bridges, and domes have survived for roughly two thousand years, while modern concrete structures sometimes deteriorate within decades. This contrast has prompted engineers to examine the composition of Roman concrete in detail.

Roman builders mixed lime with volcanic ash, which reacts chemically with lime and water to form exceptionally stable minerals. In marine structures, seawater seeping through the material appears to have encouraged the slow growth of interlocking crystals that reinforced it over time. More surprisingly, recent analyses suggest that small white lumps of lime, once dismissed as evidence of careless mixing, may have served a purpose. When cracks formed and water entered, these lumps could dissolve and recrystallize, effectively sealing the damage.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that Roman methods are simply superior. Roman concrete was considerably weaker under compression than modern formulas and was not reinforced with steel, so it could not be used for the tall, slender structures that modern cities require. Researchers are therefore not trying to reproduce ancient concrete exactly but to adapt particular features, such as self-healing behavior, to contemporary materials that must also satisfy modern demands for strength and speed of construction.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what was the original interpretation of the white lime lumps?
options: They were a deliberate reinforcement technique
They were a sign of poor mixing
They were formed by seawater
They made the concrete stronger under compression
questions.explanation: They were "once dismissed as evidence of careless mixing".

questions.stem: The phrase "effectively sealing" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: almost revealing
in practice closing
efficiently measuring
partly causing
questions.explanation: "Effectively" here means "in practice"; the recrystallized lime closes the cracks.

questions.stem: Why does the author say it would be "a mistake" to consider Roman methods simply superior?
options: Roman concrete has not actually lasted very long
Roman concrete lacks properties that modern construction needs
Volcanic ash is no longer available
Seawater damages Roman concrete over time
questions.explanation: It was weaker under compression and unreinforced, so it cannot serve tall, slender modern buildings.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about seawater's effect on Roman marine structures?
options: It gradually strengthened them
It dissolved the volcanic ash
It prevented cracks from forming
It made them weaker than land structures
questions.explanation: Seawater encouraged crystal growth that "reinforced it over time".

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the goal of current researchers?
options: To recreate Roman concrete exactly
To prove that modern concrete is better in all respects
To borrow selected Roman features for modern materials
To replace steel reinforcement with lime
questions.explanation: They aim "to adapt particular features, such as self-healing behavior, to contemporary materials".

exercises.title: The Replication Problem in Psychology
exercises.passage:
In the past two decades, large collaborative projects have attempted to repeat well-known psychological experiments, and a substantial proportion of the original findings failed to reappear. These results have been described as a crisis, but researchers disagree about what they reveal.

One explanation emphasizes questionable research practices. If investigators test many variables, stop collecting data once a result looks significant, or report only the analyses that worked, the published literature will contain an inflated number of false positives. A second explanation is less accusatory: many original studies were small, and small studies produce estimates that vary widely by chance. When journals favor striking results, the studies that happened to overestimate an effect are the ones most likely to be published, so later replications naturally find smaller effects.

A third view holds that some failures reflect genuine differences between populations, settings, or procedures rather than errors in the original work. Although this argument is sometimes used defensively, it identifies a real limitation: an effect observed among one group of students at one university may depend on conditions nobody thought to record. Reforms such as registering hypotheses in advance and sharing data address the first two explanations, but the third demands more careful theories about when an effect should occur.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Competing explanations for why many findings were not replicated
Evidence that most psychological research is fraudulent
The history of collaborative research projects
Methods for designing larger experiments
questions.explanation: The passage presents three explanations and how reforms relate to them.

questions.stem: According to the second explanation, why do replications tend to find smaller effects?
options: Replication teams use less sensitive methods
Published original studies disproportionately overestimated the effects
Participants have changed over time
Researchers deliberately manipulated their data
questions.explanation: Small, noisy studies that happened to overestimate effects were more likely to be published, so honest replications find smaller effects.

questions.stem: The word "accusatory" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: blaming
technical
optimistic
detailed
questions.explanation: The first explanation blames researchers' practices; the second is "less accusatory", i.e. assigns less blame.

questions.stem: What is the author's attitude toward the third view?
options: Completely dismissive, because it excuses poor research
Qualified acceptance: it can be misused but points to a genuine issue
Enthusiastic: it fully resolves the crisis
Neutral: the author does not evaluate it
questions.explanation: "Although this argument is sometimes used defensively, it identifies a real limitation" — a concession followed by acceptance.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about pre-registering hypotheses?
options: It would solve all three problems described
It does not, by itself, address differences between populations or settings
It makes small studies unnecessary
It is opposed by most researchers
questions.explanation: Such reforms address the first two explanations, "but the third demands more careful theories".

exercises.title: Photography and the Status of Painting
exercises.passage:
When photography became widely available in the mid-nineteenth century, some critics predicted the decline of painting. If a machine could record appearances more accurately and cheaply than any artist, they reasoned, portrait and landscape painters would soon lose their customers.

The prediction was partly correct. Many miniature portrait painters, whose trade depended on providing likenesses, either abandoned their work or became photographers themselves. Yet painting as a whole did not disappear. Instead, a number of artists began to explore what photography could not easily do. Early photographs were monochrome, and long exposure times made it difficult to capture movement, so painters increasingly emphasized color, visible brushwork, and the fleeting effects of light. Some historians argue that these developments contributed to movements such as Impressionism.

The relationship was not simply competitive, however. Painters used photographs as studies, and photographers borrowed the compositions and subjects of academic painting to gain artistic respectability. The new medium thus did not merely replace an older one; it forced both to reconsider what each could uniquely offer.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which group of artists was most directly harmed by photography?
options: Landscape painters
Miniature portrait painters
Impressionist painters
Academic painters
questions.explanation: Miniature portraitists depended on providing likenesses, which photography supplied more cheaply.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention long exposure times?
options: To explain why early photographs were expensive
To identify a limitation that painters could exploit
To argue that photography was not a real art form
To describe how Impressionists made photographs
questions.explanation: Photography struggled to capture movement, so painters emphasized what it could not do.

questions.stem: The word "fleeting" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: brief
bright
natural
distant
questions.explanation: Fleeting effects of light last only a short time.

questions.stem: What does the final paragraph suggest about photographers in this period?
options: They rejected the traditions of painting
They sought prestige by imitating established painting
They were mostly former Impressionists
They avoided portrait subjects
questions.explanation: They borrowed academic compositions "to gain artistic respectability".

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's overall view?
options: Photography destroyed painting as a profession
Photography had no real effect on painting
Photography led both media to redefine their distinctive strengths
Painting influenced photography but not the reverse
questions.explanation: The conclusion: the new medium "forced both to reconsider what each could uniquely offer".

exercises.title: Why Cities Grow Where They Do
exercises.passage:
Economic geographers distinguish between two kinds of advantage that explain where cities emerge. First-nature advantages are physical: a natural harbor, a navigable river, fertile land, or a mountain pass. Second-nature advantages arise from the concentration of people and firms itself. Once a place is large, it offers a deep pool of workers, many specialized suppliers, and opportunities for ideas to spread through face-to-face contact, all of which attract still more activity.

The interaction between these forces raises a historical question: do cities persist because their original physical advantages endure, or because concentration becomes self-sustaining? A revealing test comes from portage sites in North America, places where boats once had to be carried around waterfalls or rapids. These locations mattered for river transport in the nineteenth century, yet the advantage vanished when railroads replaced waterways. Many portage towns nevertheless remain larger today than comparable places nearby.

This persistence suggests that an initial advantage, even one that later becomes irrelevant, can lock in a city's position. The finding has implications for policy. If concentration is self-reinforcing, temporary investments might create lasting centers; however, the same logic implies that a declining city may struggle to recover once its scale begins to erode.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a second-nature advantage?
options: A river that ships can navigate
A large supply of skilled workers in a city
A natural harbor protected from storms
Fertile soil in the surrounding region
questions.explanation: Second-nature advantages arise from concentration itself, such as a deep pool of workers.

questions.stem: Why does the author discuss portage sites?
options: To show how railroads were built
To provide a case in which a physical advantage disappeared while the city remained
To argue that rivers are the most important first-nature advantage
To explain why waterfalls attract tourists
questions.explanation: Portage towns lost their transport advantage yet stayed larger — a test of persistence.

questions.stem: The phrase "lock in" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: make permanent
make secret
make illegal
make visible
questions.explanation: An early advantage fixes the city's position durably.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the final paragraph?
options: Temporary investment never affects city size
Self-reinforcing growth can work in both directions
Declining cities usually recover quickly
Physical advantages matter more than concentration
questions.explanation: The same logic that creates lasting centers implies that shrinking scale can lead to further decline.

questions.stem: How does the second paragraph relate to the first?
options: It introduces a question about the two forces and a way to test it
It rejects the distinction made in the first paragraph
It lists additional first-nature advantages
It summarizes the policy implications
questions.explanation: After defining the two advantages, the passage asks which explains persistence and offers the portage test.

exercises.title: How Plants Defend Themselves
exercises.passage:
Plants cannot run from the animals that eat them, but they are far from defenseless. Some protections are permanent features, such as thorns, tough leaves, or bitter chemicals stored in their tissues. Others are produced only when needed. When a caterpillar begins to chew a leaf, many plants respond within hours by making substances that are difficult to digest, so the insect grows more slowly and may move elsewhere.

Producing these chemicals requires energy that could otherwise be used for growth and seeds. This cost explains why many defenses are switched on only after an attack begins instead of being maintained constantly.

A damaged plant may also release scented compounds into the air. These signals serve two purposes. They attract wasps and other predators that feed on the caterpillars, and they are detected by neighboring plants, which start preparing their own defenses before any insect arrives. Scientists once doubted this second effect, since it seemed to benefit competitors. One explanation is that the signal evolved mainly to warn distant branches of the same plant, and that neighbors simply take advantage of it.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The reasons why insects prefer to feed on some plants rather than others
The ways in which plants compete with their neighbors for light and water
The different ways in which plants protect themselves from being eaten
The chemical differences between the leaves and the seeds of plants
questions.explanation: The passage describes permanent defenses, defenses produced on demand, and airborne signals.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do many plants produce defensive chemicals only after an attack begins?
options: The chemicals are harmful to the plant itself
Making them uses energy needed for growth and reproduction
Insects quickly become used to the chemicals
The chemicals are effective for only a few hours
questions.explanation: Producing them "requires energy that could otherwise be used for growth and seeds", and "this cost explains why" they are switched on only when needed.

questions.stem: The word "release" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: take in
give off
break down
hold back
questions.explanation: The plant sends scented compounds out into the air.

questions.stem: The phrase "this second effect" in the third paragraph refers to
options: wasps being attracted to the caterpillars
caterpillars growing more slowly
plants storing bitter chemicals in their tissues
neighboring plants detecting the signals and preparing defenses
questions.explanation: The two purposes are attracting predators and being "detected by neighboring plants"; scientists doubted the second.

questions.stem: Why did scientists find it hard to believe that plants warn their neighbors?
options: The scented compounds were too faint for instruments to measure
Wasps and other predators were thought to ignore signals from plants
Neighboring plants were believed to have no defenses of their own
Helping rival plants would not seem to benefit the plant sending the signal
questions.explanation: They doubted the effect "since it seemed to benefit competitors".

exercises.title: Living Beside Volcanoes
exercises.passage:
Volcanoes are among the most dangerous features of the landscape, yet hundreds of millions of people choose to live near them. The main reason lies in the ground itself. The ash and rock thrown out during eruptions contain minerals such as potassium and phosphorus that plants need. As this material breaks down, it forms deep, loose soil that holds water well. On the slopes of volcanoes in Indonesia, Italy and Central America, farmers can harvest two or three crops a year.

This fertility does not appear at once. Fresh lava is hard and almost lifeless, and it may take centuries of weathering before crops can grow on it. Fine ash, by contrast, can enrich fields within a few years, provided that the layer is thin. A thick layer buries plants and can ruin farmland for a generation.

The same eruptions that renew the soil therefore also threaten those who depend on it. Most volcanoes, however, erupt violently only once in several lifetimes, while the benefits of rich soil are felt every season. For many farming communities, an uncertain danger in the distant future weighs less than a reliable harvest today.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To explain why people settle near volcanoes despite the danger
To describe how volcanic eruptions can be predicted
To compare farming methods in three regions
To warn farmers against living on volcanic slopes
questions.explanation: The passage asks why "hundreds of millions of people choose to live near them" and answers with soil fertility weighed against rare eruptions.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what makes volcanic soil good for farming?
options: It is warmer than other soils
It contains few stones
It needs no weathering before use
It is rich in minerals and holds water well
questions.explanation: Volcanic material contains "minerals such as potassium and phosphorus" and forms soil "that holds water well".

questions.stem: How does the second paragraph relate to the first?
options: It gives further examples of regions where volcanic soil is farmed
It explains why eruptions throw out both fine ash and solid rock
It argues that volcanic soil is less fertile than farmers believe
It qualifies the claim about fertility by explaining when and how it develops
questions.explanation: After praising volcanic soil, the passage adds that "this fertility does not appear at once" and differs for lava, thin ash and thick ash.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a field covered by a thick layer of ash?
options: It will become fertile within a few years
It will turn into hard lava
It will no longer hold water
It will be unproductive for many years
questions.explanation: Ash helps "provided that the layer is thin"; a thick layer "can ruin farmland for a generation".

questions.stem: The word "reliable" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: dependable
large
early
profitable
questions.explanation: A harvest that comes every season can be counted on, unlike an uncertain danger.

exercises.title: Why the Moon Shows Only One Face
exercises.passage:
Observers on Earth always see the same side of the Moon. This is not because the Moon does not rotate. It turns on its axis exactly once during each orbit around Earth, so the same hemisphere is constantly directed toward us. The match between the two motions is no coincidence.

Billions of years ago, the Moon spun much faster. Earth's gravity pulled more strongly on the near side of the Moon than on the far side, stretching it slightly into an oval shape. As the Moon rotated, this bulge was repeatedly carried away from the line between the two bodies, and Earth's gravity pulled it back. The effect worked like a brake, gradually slowing the rotation until the bulge remained permanently aligned with Earth. Astronomers call this condition tidal locking.

The process is common. Most large moons in the solar system are locked to their planets in the same way. It also operates in the opposite direction: the Moon's pull is slowing Earth's rotation, lengthening the day by about two thousandths of a second per century. Given enough time, Earth would keep one face turned toward the Moon as well, although the Sun will have changed dramatically long before that could happen.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
options: It does not rotate on its axis as it travels around Earth
Its rotation takes the same time as its orbit around Earth
Its far side never receives any light from the Sun
Earth's rotation takes the same time as the Moon's orbit
questions.explanation: The Moon "turns on its axis exactly once during each orbit around Earth".

questions.stem: Why does the author compare the effect of Earth's gravity to "a brake"?
options: To show that the Moon's orbit is becoming smaller
To suggest that the Moon will eventually stop orbiting
To emphasize how suddenly the Moon's rotation changed
To help explain how the Moon's rotation was gradually slowed
questions.explanation: The comparison clarifies the mechanism: gravity pulling the bulge back was "gradually slowing the rotation".

questions.stem: The word "coincidence" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: accident
mystery
exception
illusion
questions.explanation: The match is not a matter of chance; the next paragraph explains its cause.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about Earth's day in the distant past?
options: It was shorter than it is today
It was the same length as today
It was longer than it is today
It matched the Moon's orbit
questions.explanation: The Moon "is slowing Earth's rotation, lengthening the day", so earlier days were shorter.

questions.stem: What is the function of the third paragraph?
options: It extends the explanation to other moons and to Earth itself
It presents evidence against tidal locking
It describes how the Moon was formed
It summarizes the two motions described in the first paragraph
questions.explanation: It states that "the process is common" among moons and "also operates in the opposite direction" on Earth.

exercises.title: The Box That Changed Trade
exercises.passage:
Until the 1950s, loading a cargo ship was slow and expensive work. Goods arrived at the port in sacks, barrels and wooden crates of every size, and teams of workers carried them on board piece by piece. A ship could spend as much time tied up in port as it did at sea, and theft and damage were common.

The shipping container offered a simple alternative: a steel box of standard dimensions that could be packed at a factory, sealed, and moved by truck, train and ship without being opened. Cranes could lift it in minutes. The idea itself was not new, however, and early attempts failed because each company used boxes of a different size. Only when shipping lines and governments agreed on common dimensions in the 1960s did it become worthwhile for ports to invest in the necessary cranes.

The consequences reached far beyond the docks. As the cost of moving goods fell dramatically, manufacturers found it economical to make products wherever labor and materials were cheapest and ship them across oceans. Old ports in city centers, which lacked space for containers, declined, while new ones grew on open land. Thousands of dock workers lost jobs that had existed for generations.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Containers were invented in the 1950s by a group of large shipping companies
Modern ports are safer and less exposed to theft than the ports of the past
A standardized container transformed shipping and, with it, patterns of trade and work
Governments were slow to support new technologies in the shipping industry
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the old loading method to the standard container and its wide consequences.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did early container systems fail?
options: Cranes were not strong enough to lift them
Dock workers refused to handle them
The boxes were often opened and robbed
Companies did not use boxes of the same size
questions.explanation: Early attempts failed "because each company used boxes of a different size".

questions.stem: What can be inferred about ports before the agreement on common dimensions?
options: They were owned and operated directly by the shipping companies
They refused to handle containers in order to protect dock workers
They had little reason to buy equipment that would suit only some boxes
They had already moved from city centers to open land nearby
questions.explanation: Only after the agreement "did it become worthwhile for ports to invest in the necessary cranes".

questions.stem: The word "ones" in the third paragraph refers to
options: containers
city centers
manufacturers
ports
questions.explanation: Old ports declined, "while new ones grew on open land".

questions.stem: Why does the author mention dock workers in the last sentence?
options: To explain why containers were introduced slowly
To argue that containers should not have been adopted
To show that the change brought losses as well as gains
To illustrate how dangerous loading ships had been
questions.explanation: After listing benefits, the passage notes that "thousands of dock workers lost jobs".

exercises.title: Islands as Natural Experiments
exercises.passage:
Why do some islands support hundreds of species while others hold only a handful? In the 1960s, ecologists proposed that the number is set by a balance between two processes. New species arrive from elsewhere, and species already present die out. When the two rates are equal, the total remains roughly constant even though the identity of the species keeps changing.

Two features of an island shift this balance. Distance from the mainland reduces arrivals, because fewer seeds, insects and birds complete a long sea crossing. Size affects extinction: a small island supports small populations, and small populations are easily eliminated by a storm, a disease or a few poor breeding seasons. Large islands near a continent should therefore be the richest, and small remote ones the poorest.

The theory was tested in a memorable way. Researchers removed all insects from several tiny mangrove islands and then recorded their return. Within about a year, each island had regained approximately its original number of species, yet the list of species differed from the one before.

The idea soon attracted attention beyond oceans. A patch of forest surrounded by farmland resembles an island, and the theory has been used, not without controversy, to estimate how many species a nature reserve of a given size can keep.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the theory described in the passage?
options: Islands always hold fewer species than the mainland
The number of species on an island reflects a balance between arrival and extinction
Species on small islands evolve more quickly than those elsewhere
The species found on an island never change once the balance is reached
questions.explanation: The number "is set by a balance between two processes": species arrive and species die out.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how does the size of an island influence the number of species it holds?
options: Smaller islands have smaller populations, which disappear more easily
Smaller islands receive fewer species arriving from the mainland
Larger islands are usually located closer to the mainland
Larger islands are less often struck by storms and disease
questions.explanation: "Size affects extinction: a small island supports small populations, and small populations are easily eliminated."

questions.stem: What did the mangrove experiment suggest?
options: Insects cannot return to an island once they have all been removed
The number of species is more predictable than which particular species are present
Small islands take far longer to recover than large islands do
The original species always return to an island in the same order
questions.explanation: Each island regained "approximately its original number of species, yet the list of species differed".

questions.stem: The word "remote" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: barren
recent
distant
narrow
questions.explanation: Remote islands are contrasted with those "near a continent".

questions.stem: What does the phrase "not without controversy" indicate about the use of the theory for nature reserves?
options: Some scientists dispute whether it can properly be applied there
It has been rejected by most scientists
It has proved more accurate on land than at sea
Its application to reserves has been universally welcomed
questions.explanation: The phrase signals that the extension to reserves has been debated, without saying it has been abandoned.

exercises.title: The Spacing Effect
exercises.passage:
Students preparing for an examination often read their notes several times in a single long session. The material soon feels familiar, and this familiarity is easily mistaken for learning. More than a century of research suggests a better strategy. When the same total study time is divided into shorter sessions separated by days, people remember considerably more weeks later. Psychologists call this the spacing effect.

One explanation concerns the effort of retrieval. After a delay, part of the material has been forgotten, and recalling it requires work. That work appears to strengthen the memory more than rereading something still fresh. A second explanation points to context: sessions on different days are linked to different surroundings and moods, which provides more routes back to the information.

If spacing is so effective, why is it so seldom used? Part of the answer is that cramming does succeed in the short term, so a student who studies intensively the night before may perform well the next morning. The loss becomes visible only later, when nobody is measuring it. Spaced study, moreover, feels less productive, because each session begins with the uncomfortable discovery of how much has slipped away. Learners thus tend to prefer the method that feels better over the one that works better.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is the spacing effect?
options: Better memory for material studied in familiar surroundings
Better long-term memory when study time is spread over separate sessions
The tendency to forget material soon after an examination
The feeling that material read many times is well known
questions.explanation: Dividing "the same total study time" into sessions "separated by days" means people "remember considerably more weeks later".

questions.stem: Why does forgetting between sessions help learning, according to the first explanation?
options: It removes incorrect information from memory
It allows the learner to rest between sessions
It shows the learner which material is unimportant
It makes recall demanding, and demanding recall strengthens memory
questions.explanation: Recalling partly forgotten material "requires work", and "that work appears to strengthen the memory".

questions.stem: Why does the author ask the question that opens the third paragraph?
options: To express doubt about the evidence for the spacing effect
To introduce an explanation of why an effective method is neglected
To suggest that students are unaware of the research
To criticize teachers who do not recommend spacing
questions.explanation: The question "why is it so seldom used?" is immediately followed by the reasons.

questions.stem: The word "cramming" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: studying with other people
studying without taking notes
studying intensively just before a test
studying the same subject for years
questions.explanation: The next clause describes "a student who studies intensively the night before".

questions.stem: What does the passage imply about how learners judge their own study methods?
options: They compare their results over several months
They rely on how a method feels, which can be misleading
They usually choose the more demanding method
They follow the advice of psychologists
questions.explanation: Familiarity is "mistaken for learning", and learners "prefer the method that feels better over the one that works better".

exercises.title: Relative Deprivation
exercises.passage:
It seems obvious that people who have less should be less satisfied than people who have more. Surveys repeatedly show something more complicated. Satisfaction depends less on what individuals possess than on how their situation compares with that of the people they regard as similar to themselves. Sociologists call the resulting sense of disadvantage relative deprivation.

The idea emerged from a study of American soldiers during the Second World War. Researchers were surprised to find that men in units where promotion was rapid complained more about their chances of advancement than men in units where it was rare. The explanation lay in the comparison each soldier made. Where many colleagues had been promoted, those who had not felt left behind; where almost nobody advanced, staying at the same rank seemed normal.

The concept helps to explain a pattern that puzzles observers of social unrest. Protest movements often gather strength not when conditions are at their worst but after a period of improvement, particularly if that improvement suddenly stops. Rising living standards raise expectations as well, and a gap opens between what people have and what they have come to regard as their due. Critics caution, however, that such feelings are widespread, whereas organized protest is not, so discontent alone cannot account for it.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: People's satisfaction is shaped by comparison with others and with their own expectations
People who own less are generally more satisfied than people who own more
Promotion in the army was unfairly distributed
Protest movements are caused by extreme poverty
questions.explanation: Satisfaction depends on "how their situation compares" with similar people, and later on expectations raised by improvement.

questions.stem: What did researchers find about soldiers in units where promotion was rapid?
options: They were more dissatisfied with their prospects than soldiers in other units
They were promoted more fairly than soldiers in other units
They rarely compared themselves with colleagues
They complained less than soldiers in units where promotion was rare
questions.explanation: Men in units with rapid promotion "complained more about their chances of advancement".

questions.stem: In the last sentence, the word "it" refers to
options: widespread discontent
a period of improvement
organized protest
the concept of deprivation
questions.explanation: Feelings are widespread "whereas organized protest is not, so discontent alone cannot account for it": what must be accounted for is organized protest.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why might unrest follow a period of improvement that suddenly ends?
options: Conditions have become worse than ever before
People's expectations have risen beyond what they now receive
People compare themselves with soldiers
Governments become weaker during periods of growth
questions.explanation: Improvement "raise[s] expectations", and "a gap opens between what people have and what they have come to regard as their due".

questions.stem: What is the function of the final sentence of the passage?
options: To offer further evidence for the concept
To explain how protests are organized
To reject the concept as mistaken
To point out a limit to what the concept can explain
questions.explanation: Critics note that discontent is common but protest is not, so the concept "alone cannot account for it".

exercises.title: Cooking and the Human Body
exercises.passage:
Humans are the only animals that cook, and some anthropologists believe the habit did more than improve the taste of food. Heat softens plant fibers and changes the structure of proteins and starches, so that the body extracts considerably more energy from a cooked meal than from the same food eaten raw. Chewing and digestion also take far less time and effort.

According to what is known as the cooking hypothesis, this extra energy shaped our anatomy. Compared with other apes, humans have small teeth, weak jaws and a short intestine, features poorly suited to a diet of raw leaves and meat. The energy saved on digestion, supporters argue, became available to an organ that consumes a great deal of it: the brain. They place the origin of cooking nearly two million years ago, when fossils first show smaller teeth and larger skulls.

The difficulty is one of timing. The oldest widely accepted traces of controlled fire, such as burned bones and hearths, are much younger than that. Supporters reply that the remains of small fires seldom survive and that absence of evidence is not proof of absence. Skeptics answer that other changes, including the use of stone tools to cut and pound food, could have reduced the work of chewing without any need for flames.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is one effect of cooking food?
options: It contains more protein than raw food
The body obtains more energy from it
It must be chewed for longer
It can be stored for a longer time
questions.explanation: The body "extracts considerably more energy from a cooked meal than from the same food eaten raw".

questions.stem: Why are small teeth and a short intestine relevant to the cooking hypothesis?
options: They suggest that human ancestors ate food that was easy to chew and digest
They show that early humans ate mostly raw meat
They prove that humans evolved from a different ape
They indicate that early humans needed less energy than other apes
questions.explanation: These features are "poorly suited to a diet of raw leaves and meat", which fits a softened, cooked diet.

questions.stem: The word "traces" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: signs
stories
tools
sources
questions.explanation: Burned bones and hearths are physical evidence left behind by fire.

questions.stem: How is the passage organized?
options: Two competing theories are described and one is shown to be correct
A discovery is described in the order in which it was made
A hypothesis is presented and then a problem with it is discussed
A widely held belief is shown to be a myth
questions.explanation: The first two paragraphs set out the hypothesis; the third begins "The difficulty is one of timing" and gives both sides.

questions.stem: What do skeptics suggest about stone tools?
options: They offer another explanation for the reduction in teeth and jaws
They were the tools used to light the earliest cooking fires
They appeared long after the first controlled use of fire
They made cooking faster and therefore more efficient
questions.explanation: Cutting and pounding food "could have reduced the work of chewing without any need for flames".

exercises.title: How New Languages Are Born
exercises.passage:
When groups with no common language must communicate, for trade or on plantations, they often develop a pidgin. A pidgin is a simplified system with a small vocabulary, drawn mostly from one language, and very little grammar. Speakers string words together as best they can, and no one learns it as a mother tongue.

Something remarkable may happen in the next generation. Children who grow up hearing a pidgin as their main language do not simply reproduce it. They expand it into a creole, a complete language with consistent rules for marking tense, forming questions and linking clauses. The creole typically possesses grammatical devices that were absent from the pidgin and that do not always resemble those of the parents' original languages.

Linguists disagree about where this structure comes from. Some see it as evidence that children are born with a blueprint for grammar, which they apply when the language around them is deficient. Others argue that the similarities among creoles have been exaggerated and that their features can usually be traced to the languages in contact. A much-studied case from Nicaragua has sharpened the debate. Deaf children brought together in new schools in the 1980s created a sign language of their own, and younger children who joined later made it more systematic than the older pupils had.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what distinguishes a creole from a pidgin?
options: A creole has a smaller vocabulary than a pidgin
A creole has a full grammar and is acquired as a first language
A creole is used only for trade
A creole is based on several languages instead of one
questions.explanation: A creole is "a complete language with consistent rules", developed by children for whom it is the main language; nobody learns a pidgin "as a mother tongue".

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the adults who create a pidgin?
options: They teach the pidgin to their children as a complete language
They gradually forget the languages they spoke before
They give the pidgin consistent rules for tense and questions
They continue to speak their original languages as their mother tongues
questions.explanation: "No one learns it as a mother tongue", so its adult users already have other native languages.

questions.stem: The word "deficient" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: foreign
complicated
incomplete
changing
questions.explanation: The surrounding language, a pidgin, lacks the grammar a full language has.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the sign language created in Nicaragua?
options: To show that sign languages are simpler in structure than spoken languages
To prove that pidgins also develop within deaf communities around the world
To present a case that bears on the dispute about the source of grammatical structure
To describe how the first schools for deaf children in the region were founded
questions.explanation: The case "has sharpened the debate" about where the structure comes from.

questions.stem: Which view is most directly supported by the fact that younger children made the sign language more systematic?
options: That creole features come from the languages in contact
That children themselves contribute grammatical structure
That the similarities among creoles have been exaggerated
That adults design the rules of new languages
questions.explanation: The children "created a sign language of their own", and it was the younger ones who made it "more systematic", which fits the view that children supply a "blueprint for grammar".

exercises.title: Urban Heat Islands
exercises.passage:
On a calm summer night, the center of a large city may be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. This difference, known as the urban heat island, arises mainly from the materials of which cities are built. Asphalt and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly after dark. Rural land behaves differently: plants draw water from the soil and release it through their leaves, and this evaporation consumes heat that would otherwise warm the air.

The shape of a city adds to the effect. Tall buildings on narrow streets trap warmth that would escape from open ground, and they block the winds that might carry it away. Engines, air conditioners and industry contribute waste heat of their own. Because the stored heat is released at night, the contrast with rural areas is usually greatest after sunset, not at midday.

The consequences are more than a matter of comfort. During heat waves, warm nights deny the body its chance to recover, and deaths rise, especially among the elderly. Demand for cooling increases electricity use, which adds further heat. Planners have responded with reflective roofs, street trees and parks. Trees are generally the most effective measure, though they need water and space, both of which are scarce exactly where cooling is most needed.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does rural land stay cooler than city surfaces?
options: Rural soil reflects more sunlight than asphalt
Evaporation of water from plants uses up heat
Winds are stronger in the countryside
Rural areas receive less sunlight
questions.explanation: Plants release water through their leaves, "and this evaporation consumes heat that would otherwise warm the air".

questions.stem: When would the temperature difference between a city and its surroundings probably be largest?
options: A few hours after sunset on a windless day
At midday on a hot day with a strong wind
Just after sunrise on a cold winter morning
During an afternoon rainstorm in summer
questions.explanation: The contrast "is usually greatest after sunset", and the opening refers to "a calm summer night"; wind would carry heat away.

questions.stem: How is the information in the passage organized?
options: A problem is described and several proposed solutions are rejected
Causes of a phenomenon are explained, followed by its effects and responses to it
Two cities are compared in detail to show why one is warmer
A scientific theory is presented and then shown to be mistaken
questions.explanation: Paragraphs one and two give causes; paragraph three gives "the consequences" and what planners have done.

questions.stem: The word "scarce" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: expensive
unnecessary
well protected
in short supply
questions.explanation: Water and space are hard to find in dense city centers.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about air conditioning during a heat wave?
options: It helps individuals while making the city as a whole warmer
It is the most effective response available to planners
It reduces deaths more than trees do
It has no effect on outdoor temperatures
questions.explanation: Air conditioners "contribute waste heat", and cooling demand "increases electricity use, which adds further heat".

exercises.title: The Market for Lemons
exercises.passage:
In many markets, sellers know far more about the quality of what they offer than buyers do. Economists call this situation asymmetric information, and a famous analysis of used cars shows how damaging it can be. A buyer who cannot distinguish a reliable car from a defective one, nicknamed a "lemon", will reasonably offer only an average price.

That offer, however, is too low for owners of good cars, who withdraw from the market, while it is generous for owners of lemons, who are delighted to sell. As good cars disappear, the average quality of those remaining falls, buyers lower their offers further, and still more good cars are withdrawn. In the extreme case, the market unravels until only the worst products are traded, even though buyers would gladly pay a fair price for a good car and its owner would gladly accept it.

The analysis helps explain institutions that might otherwise seem puzzling. Warranties, dealer reputations and independent inspections all serve to transmit information that buyers cannot obtain on their own. A seller who offers a long warranty signals confidence, since such a promise would be ruinous to make on a lemon. Where no such devices exist, trades that would benefit both sides simply fail to happen.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
options: Used cars are generally less reliable than buyers expect them to be
Sellers of used cars usually hide defects in order to deceive buyers
When buyers cannot judge quality, a market can collapse unless information is supplied
Warranties and inspections make used cars more expensive for buyers
questions.explanation: The passage shows how a market "unravels" under asymmetric information and how warranties, reputations and inspections "transmit information that buyers cannot obtain on their own".

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do owners of good cars leave the market?
options: The price buyers are willing to offer is less than their cars are worth
Buyers have come to prefer new cars to used ones of any quality
Independent inspections reveal hidden defects in their cars
They are not permitted to offer warranties on the cars they sell
questions.explanation: The average-price offer "is too low for owners of good cars, who withdraw from the market".

questions.stem: The word "unravels" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: expands
falls apart
settles down
reorganizes
questions.explanation: The market progressively shrinks "until only the worst products are traded".

questions.stem: Why would a long warranty be "ruinous" for the seller of a lemon?
options: Buyers would refuse a car sold with a warranty
The seller would have to pay for the many repairs a defective car will need
Warranties on defective cars are forbidden
The warranty would push the price above what buyers can pay
questions.explanation: A lemon is "a defective one"; promising to cover its failures would cost the seller heavily, which is why only a confident seller makes such a promise.

questions.stem: Why does the author point out that buyers "would gladly pay a fair price for a good car"?
options: To stress that the market fails even though a mutually beneficial trade is possible
To show that buyers of used cars are often willing to pay too much
To argue that the prices of used cars are generally set too high
To explain why defective cars continue to be sold in large numbers
questions.explanation: The clause begins "even though": the good cars disappear although both sides would welcome the trade, which the last sentence calls "trades that would benefit both sides".

exercises.title: After the Black Death
exercises.passage:
The plague that swept across Europe in the mid-fourteenth century killed somewhere between a third and a half of the population within a few years. Contemporary writers described the catastrophe in religious terms, but historians have increasingly examined its economic aftermath, which in some regions proved surprisingly favorable to those who survived.

With so many workers dead, labor became scarce while land remained plentiful. Peasants and laborers could demand higher wages or move to estates that offered better terms. Landowners responded by appealing to rulers, and in England a law of 1351 attempted to fix wages at their pre-plague level and forbid workers to leave their employers. Records of court cases show that the law was widely enforced, yet wages continued to rise, which suggests that employers themselves often broke it in order to attract labor.

The long-term consequences remain debated. In western Europe, the bargaining power of laborers contributed to the decline of serfdom, the system that bound peasants to a lord's land. In parts of eastern Europe, by contrast, landowners succeeded in imposing stricter controls over the following centuries. The same demographic shock thus led to opposite outcomes, a contrast that has led historians to look closely at differences in political institutions, the strength of towns, and the ability of peasants to resist collectively.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what was one immediate economic effect of the plague on surviving laborers?
options: They lost the land they had farmed
They could obtain higher pay and better conditions
They had to work longer hours for the same pay
They moved to the towns in large numbers
questions.explanation: "Peasants and laborers could demand higher wages or move to estates that offered better terms."

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about the law of 1351?
options: It was never applied by the courts
It was undermined by employers who were competing for workers
It succeeded in keeping wages at their earlier level
It applied only to workers in towns
questions.explanation: The law "was widely enforced, yet wages continued to rise", suggesting that "employers themselves often broke it in order to attract labor".

questions.stem: The word "aftermath" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: causes
beginning
consequences
records
questions.explanation: Historians examine what followed the catastrophe, which "proved surprisingly favorable" to survivors.

questions.stem: How does the third paragraph develop the discussion?
options: It describes the medical causes of the plague and how it spread
It argues that the plague had no lasting effect on European society
It gives further evidence that the law of 1351 failed to hold down wages
It contrasts different regional outcomes and points to factors that might explain them
questions.explanation: It sets western Europe "by contrast" with eastern Europe and lists "political institutions, the strength of towns, and the ability of peasants to resist".

questions.stem: What is the author's view of the idea that the plague by itself determined later social developments?
options: It is fully supported by the records of English court cases
It is irrelevant to the history of serfdom in western Europe
It is doubtful, because the same event produced opposite results
It has been accepted by nearly all historians of the period
questions.explanation: "The same demographic shock thus led to opposite outcomes", which is why historians look at other factors.

exercises.title: The Rise of Linear Perspective
exercises.passage:
Medieval European painters were fully capable of suggesting depth, yet they rarely tried to represent a scene as it would appear from a single fixed point. Figures were often sized according to their importance rather than their distance from the viewer, and buildings could be shown from several angles at once. These choices reflected the purpose of the images, which was to convey religious meaning, not to imitate visual experience.

In Florence in the early fifteenth century, a set of geometric rules changed this. The architect Brunelleschi is credited with demonstrating that parallel lines receding from the viewer should be drawn so that they converge at a single vanishing point, and the writer Alberti soon published a method that painters could follow. Within a generation, a convincing illusion of three-dimensional space became the expected standard in Italian painting.

It would be misleading, however, to describe the change simply as progress from error to accuracy. Strict perspective assumes a viewer with one motionless eye, which is not how people actually see. Moreover, painters who had mastered the system frequently departed from it, stretching a room or shifting the vanishing point to direct attention toward the main figure. Perspective was thus less a discovery of how the world looks than a powerful convention, one that served particular artistic and intellectual ambitions.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that medieval figures were sized "according to their importance"?
options: To show that medieval painters lacked technical skill
To explain how the vanishing point was discovered
To illustrate a mistake that Alberti corrected
To show that medieval painting pursued goals other than visual realism
questions.explanation: Such choices "reflected the purpose of the images, which was to convey religious meaning, not to imitate visual experience"; the painters were "fully capable of suggesting depth".

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did Alberti contribute?
options: A written procedure that painters could apply
The first demonstration of the vanishing point
A building designed with geometric rules
The first painting to show three-dimensional space
questions.explanation: Brunelleschi is credited with the demonstration; Alberti "published a method that painters could follow".

questions.stem: What can be inferred about painters who stretched a room or shifted the vanishing point?
options: They had not fully understood the geometric method
They were returning to medieval religious styles
They worked before Brunelleschi's demonstration
They adapted the rules deliberately to serve the composition
questions.explanation: They "had mastered the system" and departed from it "to direct attention toward the main figure".

questions.stem: The word "convention" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: natural law
formal meeting
careless habit
accepted practice
questions.explanation: Perspective is presented as a shared way of representing space, "less a discovery of how the world looks".

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's view of linear perspective?
options: It allowed painters for the first time to show the world exactly as it appears
It was abandoned soon after Alberti published his method
It was less important than the medieval approach to painting
It was an influential system of representation, not simply a more accurate way of seeing
questions.explanation: The author rejects describing it "as progress from error to accuracy" and calls it "a powerful convention".

exercises.title: Measuring the Distance to the Stars
exercises.passage:
Of all the quantities astronomers need, distance is among the hardest to obtain. A faint star may be a modest one nearby or a brilliant one very far away, and its appearance alone cannot tell us which. The most direct method relies on parallax. As Earth travels around the Sun, a nearby star seems to shift slightly against the background of much more distant ones, just as a finger held at arm's length appears to jump when viewed first with one eye and then with the other. Measuring that shift, and knowing the size of Earth's orbit, gives the distance by simple geometry.

The shifts are tiny, however, and beyond a few thousand light-years they become too small to measure reliably. For greater distances astronomers rely on so-called standard candles, objects whose true brightness is known. Certain pulsating stars are especially valuable, because the period of their pulsation is closely linked to their true brightness. By comparing how bright such a star really is with how bright it appears, astronomers can calculate how far away it must be.

Each method is calibrated using the one before it: pulsating stars close enough for parallax establish the relationship that is then applied to stars in distant galaxies. Astronomers call this chain the distance ladder. Its strength is also its weakness, since an error at any step is carried upward to every measurement that depends on it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why can't the distance of a star be judged from its appearance alone?
options: A faint star could be either a dim star nearby or a bright star far away
Stars change their brightness from one season of the year to another
Most stars are partly hidden behind other, more distant stars
Earth's motion around the Sun makes every star appear to move
questions.explanation: "A faint star may be a modest one nearby or a brilliant one very far away, and its appearance alone cannot tell us which."

questions.stem: Why does the author mention a finger held at arm's length?
options: To show how small the parallax of distant stars is
To illustrate the apparent shift on which parallax depends
To explain how the size of Earth's orbit is measured
To suggest that parallax measurements are unreliable
questions.explanation: The finger "appears to jump" when seen from two positions, "just as" a nearby star seems to shift as Earth moves.

questions.stem: The word "calibrated" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: adjusted against a known standard
replaced by something better
published for other scientists
made simpler to use
questions.explanation: Stars whose distance is known by parallax "establish the relationship" used for the next method.

questions.stem: How is the passage organized?
options: Two rival methods are compared, and one of them is finally rejected
Methods are presented in order of their range, and then the link between them is explained
Discoveries are described in the order in which astronomers made them
A problem is presented and then shown to have no reliable solution
questions.explanation: Parallax works nearby, standard candles "for greater distances", and the third paragraph explains that "each method is calibrated using the one before it".

questions.stem: What would most likely follow if the parallax distances to nearby pulsating stars turned out to be slightly too small?
options: Only measurements within a few thousand light-years would be affected
Standard candles would no longer be needed
Estimated distances to faraway galaxies would also have to be revised
The pulsation periods of those stars would change
questions.explanation: Nearby pulsating stars "establish the relationship that is then applied to stars in distant galaxies", and "an error at any step is carried upward".

exercises.title: Why Do We Age?
exercises.passage:
Natural selection favors traits that help organisms survive and reproduce, so the persistence of aging presents a puzzle. A body that gradually loses strength, fertility and resistance to disease seems an obvious disadvantage. Why has evolution not eliminated it?

The leading explanations start from a simple observation. In the wild, most animals die young from predators, accidents, starvation or infection, long before any decline due to age becomes apparent. Selection therefore acts weakly on traits whose effects appear late in life, because few individuals live long enough to express them. A harmful mutation that strikes only in old age can accumulate in a population almost unopposed.

A second argument goes further. Some genes may be actively favored precisely because they boost reproduction early, even if they cause damage later. A mechanism that speeds growth or raises fertility in youth will spread, so long as its costs arrive after most of its carriers have already reproduced. On this view, aging is not merely something selection failed to prevent; it is partly the price of advantages it promoted.

Both explanations predict that species facing fewer external dangers should evolve slower aging, and comparisons broadly agree: birds and bats, which can escape predators by flying, typically outlive ground-dwelling mammals of similar size. The prediction would be undermined if animals living in safe environments aged as quickly as those exposed to constant danger.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly concerned with?
options: The physical changes that occur in aging bodies
The ways in which animals avoid predators
The reasons why some genes increase fertility
Evolutionary explanations of why aging persists
questions.explanation: The passage asks why evolution has "not eliminated" aging and presents "the leading explanations".

questions.stem: According to the first explanation, why can mutations that cause harm late in life build up in a population?
options: The same mutations also raise fertility in young animals
Their effects are hidden by other mutations in the population
They help the animals that carry them to escape from predators
Few animals survive long enough for selection to act against them
questions.explanation: Selection acts weakly on late effects "because few individuals live long enough to express them". Increased early fertility belongs to the second argument.

questions.stem: In what way does the second argument "go further" than the first?
options: It applies to all animals, not only to those that live in the wild and die young
It holds that selection may actively favor genes that cause later damage, not merely fail to remove them
It explains aging without relying on natural selection or on genetic mutation
It shows that harmful mutations take effect earlier in life than was once believed
questions.explanation: Aging "is not merely something selection failed to prevent; it is partly the price of advantages it promoted".

questions.stem: The word "undermined" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: confirmed
explained
repeated
weakened
questions.explanation: The prediction would lose support if safe animals aged as fast as endangered ones.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention birds and bats?
options: To show that flying animals carry fewer harmful mutations
As evidence consistent with a prediction shared by both explanations
As an exception that neither explanation can account for
To illustrate how predators shorten lifespans in the wild
questions.explanation: "Both explanations predict" slower aging where dangers are fewer, "and comparisons broadly agree": flying species "typically outlive" similar ground-dwelling mammals.

exercises.title: Wolves, Elk and the Limits of a Good Story
exercises.passage:
When wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, after an absence of seventy years, the effects seemed to ripple through the entire ecosystem. Elk, which had multiplied without their main predator, were hunted again, and willows and aspens along the rivers, long stripped by browsing elk, began to recover. Ecologists described this as a trophic cascade: a change at the top of a food chain that travels downward through several levels.

The account was attractive, and versions of it spread widely, sometimes crediting wolves with restoring birds, beavers and even the course of rivers. Subsequent research has complicated it. Elk numbers also fell because of human hunting, severe winters and a growing population of bears. Some studies that reported dramatic recovery measured only the tallest young trees in each stand, which exaggerated the average change. And where decades of browsing had eliminated beavers, streams had cut deeper channels, lowering the water table so that willows struggle even when elk are absent.

None of this shows that wolves are unimportant. It suggests rather that ecosystems altered over a long period do not necessarily return to their earlier state when a missing species does. Removing a predator may set off a cascade; restoring it does not guarantee that the cascade runs in reverse.

questions.stem: What is the author's attitude toward the popular account of wolves in Yellowstone?
options: It is entirely false and has been abandoned by ecologists
It is accurate and complete in every important respect
It is of little interest to ecologists working in the park
It contains some truth but has been simplified and overstated
questions.explanation: Research "has complicated it", yet "none of this shows that wolves are unimportant".

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a reason for the decline in elk numbers?
options: Hunting of elk by people
A shortage of willows and aspens
A series of severe winters
A growing number of bears
questions.explanation: The passage lists "human hunting, severe winters and a growing population of bears"; willows and aspens are presented as what elk ate, not as a cause of their decline.

questions.stem: Why did measuring only the tallest young trees exaggerate the recovery?
options: Tall trees are the ones elk prefer to eat
The trees were measured before the wolves returned
The tallest trees were not representative of the stand as a whole
Tall trees grow only where beavers are present
questions.explanation: Measuring only the tallest trees "exaggerated the average change", so the rest of the stand had grown less.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention streams that had cut deeper channels?
options: To show how earlier changes can prevent recovery even after their cause is removed
To explain how the return of wolves changed the course of rivers
To show that beavers damage willows by building dams on streams
To show that elk prefer to feed near rivers rather than in forests
questions.explanation: Lower water tables mean "willows struggle even when elk are absent".

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the conclusion of the passage?
options: Wolves have little real effect on the ecosystems in which they live
Trophic cascades can occur only when a predator disappears from an area
Elk are the main cause of the changes observed in the park's rivers
Bringing back a predator does not by itself undo the effects of its long absence
questions.explanation: Ecosystems "do not necessarily return to their earlier state when a missing species does"; restoring a predator "does not guarantee that the cascade runs in reverse".

exercises.title: Gradual Change and Sudden Catastrophe
exercises.passage:
In the early nineteenth century, many naturalists explained the features of the earth through sudden catastrophes: floods or upheavals of a violence unknown in the present. Against this view, the geologist Charles Lyell argued that the processes visible today, such as erosion by rivers, the deposition of sediment and the slow rise of land, were sufficient, given immense periods of time, to account for everything geologists observed. His principle, later called uniformitarianism, became a foundation of the science, partly because it made the past open to study: if ancient processes resembled modern ones, they could be investigated by observing the present.

Lyell's position contained two claims that his followers did not always distinguish. One concerned method: explanations should rely on causes whose operation can be observed. The other concerned rates: geological change had always been slow and steady. The first proved enormously productive. The second has fared less well.

Twentieth-century research documented events that Lyell would have regarded as implausible. Enormous floods released by collapsing ice dams carved landscapes in the northwestern United States within days, and the impact of an asteroid sixty-six million years ago coincided with the disappearance of most dinosaurs. Modern geologists therefore accept that rare, violent events have shaped the planet. Yet they study such events with exactly the methods Lyell advocated, inferring their effects from physical processes understood today.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did uniformitarianism become so influential?
options: It explained the disappearance of the dinosaurs sixty-six million years ago
It was supported by evidence of enormous floods in the northwestern United States
It proved that geological change has always been slow and steady
It allowed scientists to investigate the past by studying processes that can be seen today
questions.explanation: It became a foundation "partly because it made the past open to study": ancient processes "could be investigated by observing the present".

questions.stem: What is the function of the second paragraph?
options: It separates Lyell's position into two claims that are then judged differently
It summarizes the catastrophist view that Lyell argued against
It provides new evidence that geological change is slow and steady
It explains why Lyell's followers eventually rejected his method
questions.explanation: It distinguishes a claim about "method" from one about "rates", and states that the first "proved enormously productive" while the second "has fared less well".

questions.stem: Which of the following would be consistent with the part of Lyell's position that the author regards as productive?
options: Assuming that all past changes happened at the same rate as present ones
Explaining an ancient flood through the way water and ice are known to behave
Attributing a landscape to forces that no longer operate anywhere
Rejecting the evidence for an asteroid impact
questions.explanation: The productive claim is about method, relying "on causes whose operation can be observed", as modern geologists do by "inferring their effects from physical processes understood today". The claim about rates is the one that "fared less well".

questions.stem: The phrase "fared less well" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: spread more slowly
been less successful
been taught less often
been harder to test
questions.explanation: The claim about slow, steady rates was contradicted by later evidence of violent events.

questions.stem: Why does the author state that modern geologists study violent events "with exactly the methods Lyell advocated"?
options: To criticize modern geologists for continuing to rely on outdated methods
To argue that violent events have mattered less than Lyell himself believed
To show that one part of Lyell's legacy remains valid although another has been abandoned
To suggest that Lyell had in fact foreseen the asteroid impact and its effects
questions.explanation: Geologists now accept violent events, rejecting the claim about rates, "yet" they keep his method.

exercises.title: The Productivity Paradox
exercises.passage:
During the 1970s and 1980s, businesses in the United States invested heavily in computers, yet the growth of productivity, the output produced per hour of work, slowed rather than accelerated. One economist famously remarked that computers could be seen everywhere except in the productivity statistics. The observation, known as the productivity paradox, prompted several competing explanations.

One holds that the benefits were real but poorly measured. Official statistics capture quantities of goods more easily than improvements in quality, convenience or variety, which are precisely what information technology often provides. A second explanation emphasizes delay. Historians of technology point out that electric motors spread through American factories in the 1890s, yet large productivity gains appeared only in the 1920s. Factories first used electricity to replace the single steam engine that drove all their machines; only later did managers redesign entire buildings around small motors placed at each workstation. On this account, the full value of a new technology depends on complementary changes in organization, skills and work practices, which take decades to develop.

Productivity did accelerate in the late 1990s, which seemed to support the second explanation. The pattern has since reappeared with newer digital technologies, however, and economists remain divided over whether the gains are merely delayed or were overestimated in the first place.

questions.stem: What does the passage refer to as the productivity paradox?
options: Computers reducing the number of hours people worked
Productivity rising faster than investment in computers
Statistics showing that computers lowered the quality of goods
Productivity growth slowing while investment in computers increased
questions.explanation: Businesses "invested heavily in computers, yet the growth of productivity... slowed rather than accelerated".

questions.stem: Why does the author discuss electric motors in factories?
options: To show that electricity was a more important invention than the computer
To argue that productivity statistics from the 1890s were unreliable
To give a case in which a technology paid off only after work was reorganized
To explain why factories eventually abandoned their steam engines
questions.explanation: Gains appeared decades later, once managers "redesign[ed] entire buildings around small motors"; this illustrates the "delay" explanation.

questions.stem: According to the first explanation, which of the following might official statistics fail to capture?
options: The number of computers businesses buy
The time customers save by banking online
The quantity of goods a factory produces
The number of hours employees work
questions.explanation: Statistics "capture quantities of goods more easily than improvements in quality, convenience or variety", and saved time is a gain in convenience.

questions.stem: The word "complementary" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: accompanying
unnecessary
opposing
inexpensive
questions.explanation: The technology's value "depends on" other changes made alongside it in organization, skills and work practices.

questions.stem: What does the final paragraph suggest about the acceleration of productivity in the late 1990s?
options: It proved that the earlier gains from computers had been overestimated
It did not settle the debate, since a similar puzzle arose with later technologies
It showed that the first explanation, about measurement, was correct
It resulted from improvements in the way productivity is measured
questions.explanation: It "seemed to support" the delay explanation, but "the pattern has since reappeared" and "economists remain divided".
